newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: OLYMPICS-TURMOIL AT THE TOP FOR SYDNEY GAMES.
newsitem.headline: OLYMPICS-TURMOIL AT THE TOP FOR SYDNEY GAMES.

text.p: Given the high casualty rate among those organising the 2000 Sydney Olympics, the latest man in charge is surprisingly optimistic about his survival prospects.

Within hours of his sudden elevation to the role of chief executive of the Sydney organising committee, former diplomat and career bureaucrat Sandy Hollway said he intended to see the task through until after the Games.
"I fully expect to be around until the end of March in the year 2001," Hollway told reporters at a news conference last week to announce his appointment.
But the history of upheaval that has plagued the Sydney Organising Committee for the Olympic Games (SOCOG) in recent years suggests Hollway may struggle to last the distance.
Three people have held the post of SOCOG president over the past 13 months and Hollway's predecessor as chief executive lasted only 19 months.
A further three senior executives, including the finance director, resigned last year and the composition of the 15-member board has also significantly changed.

Although the Games are still more than three years off, the turmoil at the top is beginning to raise concerns that Sydney's internal struggles will affect its ability to fulfil the promises it made to the International Olympic Committee (IOC).

The private consortium building the 110,000-seater Olympic stadium has added to the uncertainty after its bid to meet construction costs through a share market float flopped, leaving underwriters with a shortfall of more than A$200 million (US$156 million).
Boasting world-renowned harbour views, strong sporting tradition and virtually guaranteed sunshine, Sydney produced arguably the best Olympic bid ever to pip Beijing in Monte Carlo in 1993.
Few doubted that on October 1 2000, Sydney would hear the accolade every Olympic city dreams of -- that it had hosted the "best Games ever".
But that was before the in-fighting started and before Atlanta's unhappy Olympic experience showed just how difficult it is to organise the world's greatest peacetime event.
The IOC itself has kept out of SOCOG's travails, although one IOC official recently stressed the need for stability in the upper echelons of the organisation.
Then, a week ago, Mal Hemmerling, who ran the Australian Formula One grand prix in Adelaide for 10 years, was pushed into resigning as chief executive.

Officially, Hemmerling left to pursue other career options, although he has the cushion of one year's salary, estimated at A$500,000. Olympic insiders say he was forced out because of differences with SOCOG president Michael Knight.

With revenue from the sale of television rights for the Games higher than originally projected and no major problems with infrastructure planning or construction, there was little apparent reason for Hemmerling to depart on performance grounds.

The spotlight has turned on Knight, a cabinet minister with the New South Wales state government, who stands accused of politicising the Sydney Games and making SOCOG a virtual extension of the NSW Labour Party.

Opposition Olympics spokesman and SOCOG board member Ian Armstrong was among those who criticised Knight's approach after Hemmerling's sudden departure, saying the state government had "cleansed" SOCOG's administration.

Armstrong said Knight had also overseen a loss of corporate expertise in the organisation -- neither Knight nor Hollway are businessmen -- and weakened its official independence from the state government, which is underwriting the Olympics.

"Every time there is some indication of politicising, or management that is not in the defined and distinct interests of the Olympic Games, it leaves room for error and we cannot afford to make any mistakes," Armstrong said.
When businessman John Iliffe resigned as SOCOG president last September, Knight -- already NSW Olympics minister -- took over the position with the blessing of the IOC.
After the problems of Atlanta, which struggled to break even without any public funding, IOC chief Juan Antonio Samaranch and his aides wanted to be sure the NSW government was tied in to the Games.
But some of Knight's critics say the government is now effectively organising the Games.
And there is no certainty that the upheavals will not continue.
With the next state election due in 1999, Knight admits a defeat for Labour at the polls will mean his removal as SOCOG president in favour of a political opponent.
"Nobody can guarantee that people won't resign or drop dead. And I cannot even guarantee that my party will win the next election," Knight said.
